claim: PCGF6 interacts with RING1A/B and E2F6 associated factors to form a non-canonical PRC1 known as PCGF6-PRC1.
source: The ring finger protein PCGF6 (polycomb group ring finger 6) interacts with RING1A/B and E2F6 associated factors to form a non-canonical PRC1 (polycomb repressive complex 1) known as PCGF6-PRC1.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and is supported by mass spectrometry data showing protein-protein interactions (Figure 1A,B) and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 1C).

claim: PCGF6-PRC1 plays a role in repressing a subset of PRC1 target genes by recruiting RING1B and mediating downstream mono-ubiquitination of histone H2A.
source: Here, we demonstrate that PCGF6-PRC1 plays a role in repressing a subset of PRC1 target genes by recruiting RING1B and mediating downstream mono-ubiquitination of histone H2A.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing PCGF6 and RING1B co-localization (Figure 1D-G), ChIP-qPCR showing H2AK119ub1 enrichment at PCGF6 targets (Figure 2C), and tethering experiments (Figure 3A).

claim: PCGF6-PRC1 bound loci are highly enriched for promoters of germ cell-related genes in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source: PCGF6-PRC1 bound loci are highly enriched for promoters of germ cell-related genes in mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 1D) and gene ontology analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) showing enrichment of meiosis- and germ cell-related genes among PCGF6 targets.

claim: Conditional ablation of Pcgf6 in ESCs leads to robust de-repression of germ cell-related genes.
source: Conditional ablation of Pcgf6 in ESCs leads to robust de-repression of such germ cell-related genes, in turn affecting cell growth and viability.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing up-regulation of PCGF6 target genes in Pcgf6-KO ESCs (Figure 2A) and RT-qPCR validation (Figure 2B).

claim: Conditional ablation of Pcgf6 in ESCs affects cell growth and viability.
source: Conditional ablation of Pcgf6 in ESCs leads to robust de-repression of such germ cell-related genes, in turn affecting cell growth and viability.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation assays showing reduced growth rate in Pcgf6-KO ESCs (Figure 5A,B,D).

claim: PCGF6 has a role in pre- and peri-implantation mouse embryonic development.
source: We also find a role for PCGF6 in pre- and peri-implantation mouse embryonic development.
evidence: This claim is supported by genotype distribution data showing non-Mendelian ratios (Figure 6D), embryonic lethality observations (Figure 6E), and failure to establish ESC lines from Pcgf6-/- blastocysts (Figure 6F).

claim: A heterodimer of the transcription factors MAX and MGA recruits PCGF6 to target loci.
source: We further show that a heterodimer of the transcription factors MAX and MGA recruits PCGF6 to target loci.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR showing loss of PCGF6 binding upon Max or Mga knockdown (Figure 4C), motif enrichment analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), and co-immunoprecipitation data (Figure 1C).

claim: PCGF6 links sequence specific target recognition by the MAX/MGA complex to PRC1-dependent transcriptional silencing of germ cell-specific genes in pluripotent stem cells.
source: PCGF6 thus links sequence specific target recognition by the MAX/MGA complex to PRC1-dependent transcriptional silencing of germ cell-specific genes in pluripotent stem cells.
evidence: This claim integrates multiple lines of evidence including MAX/MGA-dependent PCGF6 recruitment (Figure 4C), PCGF6-dependent RING1B recruitment (Figure 3B,C), and gene expression changes in knockouts (Figure 2A, Figure 4B).

claim: PcG-mediated gene silencing involves H2A mono-ubiquitination at K119 by PRC1.
source: PcG-mediated gene silencing involves at least two distinct enzymatic activities directed to histone tails: the first mediates Histone H2A mono-ubiquitination at K119 (H2AK119ub1) by the polycomb repressive complexes 1 (PRC1), while the second mediates H3 tri-methylation at K27 (H3K27me3) by the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) (Cao et al., 2002; Czermin et al., 2002; Kuzmichev et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2002; Shao et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing this mechanism.

claim: PcG-mediated gene silencing involves H3 tri-methylation at K27 by PRC2.
source: PcG-mediated gene silencing involves at least two distinct enzymatic activities directed to histone tails: the first mediates Histone H2A mono-ubiquitination at K119 (H2AK119ub1) by the polycomb repressive complexes 1 (PRC1), while the second mediates H3 tri-methylation at K27 (H3K27me3) by the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) (Cao et al., 2002; Czermin et al., 2002; Kuzmichev et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2002; Shao et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing this mechanism.

claim: H3K27me3 deposition by EZH1/2 leads to binding of CBX2, facilitating recruitment of canonical PRC1.
source: According to the canonical view, H3K27me3 deposition by the EZH1/2 (enhancer of zeste homologs 1 and 2) histone methyltransferases leads to binding of the H3K27me3-reader protein CBX2 (chromobox protein homolog 2), in turn facilitating sequential recruitment of canonical PRC1 (cPRC1) (Bernstein et al., 2006; Cao et al., 2002; Czermin et al., 2002; Fischle et al., 2003; Kuzmichev et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing the canonical PRC1 recruitment model.

claim: H2AK119ub1 deposition by non-canonical PRC1 promotes downstream recruitment of PRC2 and H3K27me3.
source: Conversely, H2AK119ub1 deposition by the non-canonical PRC1 (ncPRC1) promotes downstream recruitment of PRC2 and H3K27me3 (Blackledge et al., 2014; Cooper et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature describing the non-canonical PRC1 mechanism.

claim: PCGF factors (PCGF1 to PCGF6) directly associate with RING1A/B proteins.
source: The molecular complexity underlying PcG-mediated gene silencing could be partly explained by the diversity of the PCGF factors (from PCGF1 to PCGF6) that directly associate with RING1A/B proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field and is confirmed by the co-IP data in this study (Figure 1C).

claim: Canonical PRC1 includes PCGF2 (MEL18) or PCGF4 (Bmi1).
source: For example, canonical PRC1 (cPRC1) may include PCGF2 (also known as MEL18: melanoma nuclear protein 18) or PCGF4 (also known as Bmi1: B cell-specific Moloney murine leukemia virus integration site 1).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: cPRC1 complexes can be classified into sub-complexes according to their association with CBX or PHC proteins.
source: These cPRC1 complexes can be further classified into specific sub-complexes according to their association with CBX (CBX2/4/6/7/8) or PHC (PHC1/2/3: polyhomeotic homologs 1, 2 and 3) (Gao et al., 2012; Vandamme et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CBX proteins contribute to recognition of H3K27me3 and mediate recruitment of cPRC1 to target loci.
source: CBX proteins contribute to recognition of H3K27me3, and therefore mediate recruitment of cPRC1 into target loci; while PHC proteins mediate gene compaction through polymerization of the SAM (sterile alpha motif) domain to facilitate transcriptional silencing (Isono et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PHC proteins mediate gene compaction through polymerization of the SAM domain to facilitate transcriptional silencing.
source: CBX proteins contribute to recognition of H3K27me3, and therefore mediate recruitment of cPRC1 into target loci; while PHC proteins mediate gene compaction through polymerization of the SAM (sterile alpha motif) domain to facilitate transcriptional silencing (Isono et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Non-canonical PRC1 associates with PCGF1, PCGF3, PCGF5 or PCGF6 and RYBP or YAF2.
source: Non-canonical PRC1 (ncPRC1) associates with PCGF1, PCGF3, PCGF5 or PCGF6 and RYBP (RING1 and YY1-binding protein) or YAF2 (YY1 Associated Factor 2), but does not interact with CBX2/4/6/7/8 or PHC1/2/3 (Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and confirmed by the co-IP data in this study (Figure 1C).

claim: Non-canonical PRC1 does not interact with CBX2/4/6/7/8 or PHC1/2/3.
source: Non-canonical PRC1 (ncPRC1) associates with PCGF1, PCGF3, PCGF5 or PCGF6 and RYBP (RING1 and YY1-binding protein) or YAF2 (YY1 Associated Factor 2), but does not interact with CBX2/4/6/7/8 or PHC1/2/3 (Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PCGF1-PRC1 incorporates KDM2B, BCOR, BCORL1, RYBP, YAF2 and SKP1 in addition to RING1A/B and PCGF1.
source: In addition to the core subunits RING1A/B and PCGF1, ncPRC1-containing PCGF1 (PCGF1-PRC1) also incorporates KDM2B [Lysine (K)-Specific Demethylase 2B], BCOR (BCL6 Corepressor), BCORL1 (BCL6 Corepressor-Like 1), RYBP, YAF2 and SKP1 (S-Phase Kinase-Associated Protein 1) (Farcas et al., 2012; Gearhart et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Non-canonical PRC1 complexes are functionally linked with canonical PRC1, and most of their target genes overlap.
source: Non-canonical PRC1 complexes are functionally linked with their canonical counterparts (cPRC1), and most of their target genes overlap with each other (Blackledge et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Overlapping genes between ncPRC1 and cPRC1 often possess unmethylated CpG islands in their promoters.
source: These overlapping genes often possess unmethylated CpG islands (CGI) in their promoters, and these are preferentially bound by the CXXC (two cysteines separated by two other residues) domain of KDM2B via recognition of unmethylated CpG dinucleotides (Farcas et al., 2012; He et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: KDM2B binds to unmethylated CpG islands via its CXXC domain.
source: These overlapping genes often possess unmethylated CpG islands (CGI) in their promoters, and these are preferentially bound by the CXXC (two cysteines separated by two other residues) domain of KDM2B via recognition of unmethylated CpG dinucleotides (Farcas et al., 2012; He et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: KDM2B binding allows direct recruitment of PCGF1-PRC1, followed by binding of PRC2 through recognition of H2AK119ub1.
source: KDM2B binding to target genes allows direct recruitment of PCGF1-PRC1, followed by binding of PRC2 through recognition of H2AK119ub1 (Blackledge et al., 2014; Cooper et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Non-canonical PCGF1-PRC1 can activate the PRC2-cPRC1 axis to ensure robust transcriptional silencing of developmental genes with unmethylated CGIs.
source: As PRC2 further recruits cPRC1, non-canonical PCGF1-PRC1 can therefore activate the PRC2-cPRC1 axis to ensure robust transcriptional silencing of developmental genes that harbor unmethylated CGIs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited literature and established mechanisms.

claim: PCGF6 was first identified in a multimeric protein complex associated with the E2F6 transcription factor.
source: Another PCGF homolog, PCGF6, was first identified in a multimeric protein complex associated with the E2F6 transcription factor (Ogawa et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PCGF6-PRC1 forms stable complexes with RING1A/B, PCGF6, L3MBTL2, RYBP, YAF2, G9A, GLP, and CBX1/3.
source: This complex was annotated as PCGF6-PRC1, and was shown to form stable complexes with several other well-known epigenetic factors such as RING1A/B, PCGF6, L3MBTL2 [lethal(3)malignant brain tumor-like 2], RYBP, YAF2, G9A (also known as EHMT2: euchromatic histone-lysine N-methyltransferase 2), GLP (G9a-like protein 1, also known as EHMT1), and CBX1/3 (Gao et al., 2012; Hauri et al., 2016; Kloet et al., 2016; Ogawa et al., 2002; Qin et al., 2012; Trojer et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by mass spectrometry data in this study (Figure 1B).

claim: PCGF6-PRC1 interacts with sequence-specific DNA binding proteins such as E2F6, MAX, MGA and TFDP1.
source: Interestingly, PCGF6-PRC1 also interacts with sequence-specific DNA binding proteins such as E2F6, MAX, MGA and TFDP1 (transcription factor Dp-1) (Gao et al., 2012; Hauri et al., 2016; Kloet et al., 2016; Ogawa et al., 2002; Qin et al., 2012; Trojer et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by mass spectrometry and co-IP data in this study (Figure 1B,C).

claim: DNA binding proteins could play a role in sequence specific recruitment of PCGF6-PRC1 to target loci.
source: This suggests that such DNA binding proteins could play a role in sequence specific recruitment of PCGF6-PRC1 to target loci; however, this notion has not been experimentally validated.
evidence: This claim is speculative based on the composition of the complex, and the authors note it had not been experimentally validated prior to this study.

claim: PCGF6 mediates repression of target genes by recruiting RING1B and facilitating H2AK119ub1.
source: We demonstrate that PCGF6 mediates repression of target genes by recruiting RING1B and facilitating H2AK119ub1.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq showing RING1B loss at PCGF6 targets in Pcgf6-KO (Figure 3B,C), ChIP-qPCR showing H2AK119ub1 loss (Figure 2C), and tethering experiments (Figure 3A).

claim: PCGF6 and RING1B common targets are enriched for meiosis- and germ cell-related genes in ESCs.
source: Taking advantage of a Pcgf6 conditional allele, we show that PCGF6 and RING1B common targets are enriched for meiosis- and germ cell-related genes in ESCs, and that such genes are robustly de-repressed in the absence of PCGF6 (Pcgf6-KO).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 1D-G) and gene ontology analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Silencing of germ cell-related genes by PCGF6 plays a role in proliferation and growth of ESCs.
source: Importantly, silencing of germ cell-related genes by PCGF6 likely plays a role in proliferation and growth of ESCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation assays showing reduced growth in Pcgf6-KO ESCs (Figure 5A,B,D) and the observation that germ cell genes are de-repressed in these cells (Figure 2A,B).

claim: Loss of Pcgf6 leads to pleiotropic defects in vivo, including aberrant axial development and impaired placenta formation.
source: Indeed, loss of Pcgf6 leads to pleiotropic defects in vivo, including aberrant axial development and impaired placenta formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by skeletal analysis showing axial transformations (Figure 6G,H) and histological analysis showing placental defects (Figure 6J,K).

claim: PCGF6-PRC1 utilizes MGA and MAX as a heterodimeric DNA binding module to directly recognize and repress expression of germ cell- and meiosis-related genes.
source: We also reveal a unique recruitment mechanism amongst PRC1 complexes whereby PCGF6-PRC1 utilizes its MGA and MAX components as a heterodimeric DNA binding module to directly recognize and repress expression of germ cell- and meiosis-related genes to support ESC maintenance and embryonic development.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), ChIP-qPCR showing MAX/MGA-dependent PCGF6 recruitment (Figure 4C), and gene expression changes in Max/Mga knockdowns (Figure 4B).

claim: The mouse ESC PCGF6 complex is similar to those purified from human cells.
source: We observed strong association of PCGF6 with MGA, RING1B, RING1A, CBX3, CBX1, RYBP, L3MBTL2, YAF2 and TFDP1 (Figure 1A,B), indicating that the mouse ESC PCGF6 complex is similar to those purified from human cells (Gao et al., 2012; Hauri et al., 2016; Kloet et al., 2016; Ogawa et al., 2002; Trojer et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from this study (Figure 1A,B) compared with cited literature on human PCGF6 complexes.

claim: MAX was not detected in considerable amounts in the PCGF6 complexes in mouse ESCs by mass spectrometry.
source: We however did not detect considerable amounts of MAX in the PCGF6 complexes in mouse ESCs.
evidence: This claim is based on the mass spectrometry data (Figure 1B) where MAX is not listed among the detected proteins.

claim: MAX protein associates with FLAG-PCGF6 as detected by immunoprecipitation-immunoblotting.
source: We indeed found considerable association of MAX with both FLAG-PCGF6 and FLAG-RING1B as well as the other three proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PCGF1 and PCGF2 do not co-immunoprecipitate with FLAG-PCGF6.
source: We further observed PCGF1 or PCGF2 was not co-IPed with FLAG-PCGF6 while both of them associated with FLAG-RING1B.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: EZH2 and SET1 do not co-immunoprecipitate with FLAG-PCGF6 or FLAG-RING1B.
source: We finally confirmed EZH2 or SET1 were not co-IPed with either FLAG-PCGF6 or FLAG-RING1B.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PCGF6 is primarily involved in non-canonical PRC1 (ncPRC1), particularly PCGF6-PRC1, in mouse ESCs.
source: These results suggested that PCGF6 would be primarily involved in non-canonical PRC1 (ncPRC1), particularly PCGF6-PRC1, in mouse ESCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-IP data showing PCGF6 associates with ncPRC1 components but not with cPRC1-specific components like PCGF2 (Figure 1C).

claim: Genetic ablation of Ring1A/B leads to widespread disruption of PRC1-dependent gene repression.
source: Consistent with this model, it has been shown that genetic ablation of Ring1A/B leads to widespread disruption of PRC1-dependent gene repression (de Napoles et al., 2004; Endoh et al., 2008; Leeb and Wutz, 2007; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PCGF6 binds to the transcriptional start sites of genes associated with germ cell specific functions.
source: This analysis revealed that PCGF6 bound to the transcriptional start sites (TSSs) of a group of genes associated with germ cell specific functions, such as Tex19.1 (testis-expressed protein 19A) and Tdrkh (Tudor and KH domain containing) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Genes bound by PCGF6 are also marked by RING1B.
source: Indeed, these genes were also marked by RING1B, indicating that PCGF6 and RING1B share common targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1D and the Venn diagram in Figure 1E.

claim: cPRC1 targets, such as the Hoxd gene cluster, are not bound by PCGF6.
source: Intriguingly, cPRC1 targets, such as the Hoxd (homeobox protein Hox-D) gene cluster, were not bound by PCGF6 (Figure 1D), indicating that PCGF6 might associate with a subset of RING1B-bound genes that are not marked by cPRC1.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 1218 genes in ESCs are bound by PCGF6.
source: A detailed examination of ChIP-seq datasets revealed that 1218, 2959 and 4946 genes in ESCs were bound by PCGF6, RING1B, and H3K27me3, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 2959 genes in ESCs are bound by RING1B.
source: A detailed examination of ChIP-seq datasets revealed that 1218, 2959 and 4946 genes in ESCs were bound by PCGF6, RING1B, and H3K27me3, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 4946 genes in ESCs are marked by H3K27me3.
source: A detailed examination of ChIP-seq datasets revealed that 1218, 2959 and 4946 genes in ESCs were bound by PCGF6, RING1B, and H3K27me3, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PCGF6-bound genes partially but significantly overlap with both RING1B and H3K27me3 target genes.
source: As expected, PCGF6-bound genes partially but significantly overlapped with both RING1B and H3K27me3 target genes (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: PCGF6 target sites exhibit only a limited overlap with CBX7.
source: PCGF6 target sites, however, exhibited only a limited overlap with CBX7, supporting the model in which PCGF6 is predominantly involved in ncPRC1.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PCGF6 binds in close proximity to TSS, unlike RING1B, CBX7 and H3K27me3 which exhibit a broader distribution.
source: This analysis revealed that PCGF6 bound in close proximity to TSS, unlike RING1B, CBX7 and H3K27me3, all of which exhibited a broader distribution (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: MAX associates considerably with PCGF6 targets irrespective of RING1B binding.
source: We observed considerable association of MAX at PCGF6 targets irrespective of RING1B binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: H3K27me3 deposition at PCGF6 targets is mainly seen at RING1B-bound genes.
source: In contrast, H3K27me3 deposition at PCGF6 targets was mainly seen at RING1B-bound genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: PCGF6 target genes harbor CGIs that tend to be slightly shorter and more methylated than CBX7 targets.
source: We also noted that PCGF6 target genes harbor CGIs that tend to be slightly shorter and more methylated than CBX7 targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: PCGF6 targets are bound by KDM2B.
source: Consistently, PCGF6 targets were bound by KDM2B.
evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: KDM2B loss induces a subtle increase of RING1B binding at PCGF6 targets.
source: KDM2B loss induced a subtle increase of RING1B binding at PCGF6 targets while RING1B binding at CBX7 targets was marginally decreased (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: PCGF6-bound genes are up-regulated to a much lesser extent than CBX7-bound genes in Kdm2b-KO ESCs.
source: Moreover, PCGF6-bound genes were up-regulated to a much lesser extent than CBX7-bound genes in Kdm2b-KO ESCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: CGI recognition by KDM2B has distinct roles for PCGF6-PRC1 recruitment from that reported for cPRC1.
source: These results suggest that the CGI recognition by KDM2B has distinct roles for PCGF6-PRC1 recruitment from that reported for cPRC1 (Farcas et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing different effects of KDM2B loss on PCGF6 vs CBX7 targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G) compared to the cited literature.

claim: More than 250 genes are considerably up-regulated in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
source: To test this, we performed RNA-seq and found that more than 250 genes were considerably up-regulated in Pcgf6-KO ESCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Genes up-regulated in Pcgf6-KO ESCs are a subset of genes up-regulated in Ring1A/B-dKO ESCs.
source: Importantly, these genes were a subset of the genes up-regulated in the Ring1A and Ring1B double knockout (Ring1A/B-dKO) ESCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PCGF6+RING1B+ genes are barely transcribed in WT ESCs.
source: This analysis showed that the PCGF6+RING1B+ genes were barely transcribed in WT ESCs; likewise, the PCGF6-RING1B+ genes were marginally expressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by the FPKM analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PCGF6+RING1B- genes that harbor CGIs are robustly expressed in WT ESCs.
source: In contrast, the PCGF6+RING1B- group that harbors CGIs was robustly expressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by the FPKM analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both PCGF6+RING1B+ and PCGF6-RING1B+ genes are significantly up-regulated in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
source: We found both PCGF6+RING1B+ and PCGF6-RING1B+ genes were significantly up-regulated while expression levels of PCGF6+RING1B- or PCGF6-RING1B- genes were barely altered in Pcgf6-KO ESCs (Figure 2A, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by the dot plot analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Expression levels of PCGF6+RING1B- or PCGF6-RING1B- genes are barely altered in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
source: We found both PCGF6+RING1B+ and PCGF6-RING1B+ genes were significantly up-regulated while expression levels of PCGF6+RING1B- or PCGF6-RING1B- genes were barely altered in Pcgf6-KO ESCs (Figure 2A, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by the dot plot analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Expression levels of highly up-regulated genes in the PCGF6+RING1B+ category are considerably higher than those in the PCGF6-RING1B+ category in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
source: We however also found that expression levels of highly up-regulated genes (more than 5-times; indicated by red lines in Figure 2A) in the PCGF6+RING1B+ category were considerably higher than those in the PCGF6-RING1B+ category in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dot plot analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PCGF6+RING1B+ and PCGF6-RING1B+ categories are also up-regulated in Ring1A/B-dKO ESCs.
source: Those categories were also up-regulated in Ring1A/B-dKO ESCs (Figure 2A, right), suggesting a functional link between PCGF6 and RING1A/B for down-regulation of such genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dot plot analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PCGF6 contributes to RING1B-mediated repression of target genes primarily in the PCGF6+RING1B+ category.
source: Together, PCGF6 is suggested to contribute to RING1B-mediated repression of target genes primarily in the PCGF6+RING1B+ category but also in RING1B targets not bound by PCGF6 to a lesser extent.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the gene expression data in Figure 2A and RT-qPCR validation in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: PCGF6-PRC1 target genes are enriched in meiosis- and germ cell-related genes.
source: To gain insight into the physiological role of PCGF6-PRC1-mediated gene regulation in ESCs, we performed gene ontology (GO) analyses, which revealed that PCGF6-PRC1 target genes are enriched in meiosis- and germ cell-related genes as suggested previously (Zdzieblo et al., 2014), unlike the cPRC1 target genes that are predominantly enriched in developmental genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: cPRC1 target genes are predominantly enriched in developmental genes.
source: To gain insight into the physiological role of PCGF6-PRC1-mediated gene regulation in ESCs, we performed gene ontology (GO) analyses, which revealed that PCGF6-PRC1 target genes are enriched in meiosis- and germ cell-related genes as suggested previously (Zdzieblo et al., 2014), unlike the cPRC1 target genes that are predominantly enriched in developmental genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: PCGF6-PRC1 has a potential role for suppression of the meiotic program or germ cell differentiation program in ESCs.
source: These results suggest a potential role of PCGF6-PRC1 for suppression of the meiotic program or germ cell differentiation program, or both, in ESCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the GO analysis showing enrichment of meiosis and germ cell genes among PCGF6 targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claim: H2AK119ub1 is considerably enriched at PCGF6-PRC1 target genes.
source: Indeed, ChIP-qPCR analyses revealed considerable enrichment of H2AK119ub1 at PCGF6-PRC1 target genes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: H2AK119ub1 enrichment at PCGF6-PRC1 target genes is dramatically diminished in the absence of Pcgf6.
source: Furthermore, this H2AK119ub1 enrichment was dramatically diminished in the absence of Pcgf6, revealing a role for PCGF6 in mediating H2AK119ub1 deposition (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: H2AK119ub1 enrichment at cPRC1 targets (Zic1 and Hoxd11) is marginally affected in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
source: In contrast, H2AK119ub1 enrichment at Zic1 and Hoxd11, cPRC1 targets, was marginally affected in Pcgf6-KO ESCs, further supporting our model that PCGF6 is not primarily involved in cPRC1-dependent repression (Figure 2C, middle).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mutations of RING1B residue I53 (I53S or I53A) abrogate its E3 ligase activity by disrupting interactions with UBCH5C.
source: Previous reports have demonstrated that mutations of RING1B residue I53 (i.e., I53S or I53A), abrogated its E3 ligase activity by disrupting its interactions with the E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme UBCH5C (also known as UBE2D3: Ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme E2 D3) (Ben-Saadon et al., 2006; Buchwald et al., 2006; Endoh et al., 2012; Eskeland et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rescuing Ring1A/B-dKO cells with I53 mutants fails to maintain transcriptional repression of PCGF6 target genes.
source: Rescuing the Ring1A/B-dKO cells with the I53 mutants failed to maintain transcriptional repression, demonstrating that repression of PCGF6 target genes depends on the catalytic activity of RING1B and likely also downstream H2AK119ub1 deposition (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Repression of PCGF6 target genes depends on the catalytic activity of RING1B and downstream H2AK119ub1 deposition.
source: Rescuing the Ring1A/B-dKO cells with the I53 mutants failed to maintain transcriptional repression, demonstrating that repression of PCGF6 target genes depends on the catalytic activity of RING1B and likely also downstream H2AK119ub1 deposition (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data showing that catalytically inactive RING1B mutants cannot rescue repression (Figure 2D).

claim: H2AK119ub1 plays a critical role for recruitment of PRC2 and downstream H3K27me3 deposition.
source: Since our previous report demonstrated that H2AK119ub1 plays a critical role for recruitment of PRC2 and downstream H3K27me3 deposition (Blackledge et al., 2014), we thus investigated H3K27me3 deposition at the representative PCGF6 bound genes, and indeed found a significant H3K27me3 enrichment at these targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work and ChIP-qPCR data in this study (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: H3K27me3 deposition at PCGF6-PRC1 targets is mediated by the PRC2 complex.
source: As expected, the H3K27me3 level was markedly reduced in the absence of the key PRC2 component EED (embryonic ectoderm development), confirming that H3K27me3 deposition in these genes is mediated by the PRC2 complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing loss of H3K27me3 in Eed-KO ESCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claim: H3K27me3 level at PCGF6-PRC1 targets is considerably reduced in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
source: We indeed found a considerable reduction in H3K27me3 level at these PCGF6-PRC1 targets in Pcgf6-KO ESCs, but only marginally at cPRC1 targets, suggesting a potential role for PCGF6-mediated H2AK119ub1 to recruit PRC2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PRC2-mediated mechanisms exhibit only limited impact on the repression of PCGF6-PRC1 targets.
source: However, consistent with a previous report (Riising et al., 2014), PRC2-mediated mechanisms exhibited only limited impact on the repression of PCGF6-PRC1 targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data in Eed-KO ESCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) and a citation to previous literature.

claim: PCGF6 physically interacts with RING1B through its RING finger domain.
source: Previous studies have reported that PCGF6 interacts with RING1B through its RING finger domain (Akasaka et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Ectopic targeting of PCGF6/TETR fusion protein to a TetO array leads to sequential binding of RING1B, H2AK119ub1 deposition and PRC2 recruitment.
source: ChIP-qPCR analysis showed binding of the PCGF6/TETR fusion protein at the TetO array. Importantly, this was accompanied by considerable enrichment of RING1B, MAX and H2AK119ub1, indicating that PCGF6 recruits PCGF6-PRC1 (Figure 3A). We also observed association of EZH2 and H3K27me3 with the TetO array, likely mediated by the upstream H2AK119ub1 as reported previously (Blackledge et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data from the tethering experiment shown in Figure 3A.

claim: RING1B binding to PCGF6-PRC1 target genes is considerably depleted in the absence of Pcgf6.
source: This experiment demonstrated that RING1B binding to PCGF6-PRC1 target genes such as Tex19.1, Tdrkh, Syce1 (synaptonemal complex central element protein 1) and Mael (maelstrom spermatogenic transposon silencer) was indeed considerably depleted in the absence of Pcgf6 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RING1B binding to cPRC1 target sites, such as the Hoxb cluster, is unaffected in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
source: In contrast, RING1B binding to cPRC1 target sites, such as the Hoxb cluster, was unaffected.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RING1B binding to core PCGF6-PRC1 target genes (PCGF6+CBX7-RING1B+) is considerably reduced in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
source: We observed considerable reduction of RING1B binding to the core PCGF6-PRC1 target genes (PCGF6+CBX7-RING1B+) in Pcgf6-KO (green dot plots in Figure 3C, left; green lines in Figure 3C, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: cPRC1 target genes (PCGF6-CBX7+RING1B+) are not affected by Pcgf6 deletion.
source: In contrast, cPRC1 target genes (PCGF6-CBX7+RING1B+) were not affected.
evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Genetic ablation of Pcgf2 (Mel18) and Pcgf4 (Bmi1) leads to reduction of RING1B binding only at cPRC1 target genes.
source: Consistent with these observations, genetic ablation of Pcgf2 (Mel18) and Pcgf4 (Bmi1), both of which are essential components of the cPRC1 complex, led to reduction of RING1B binding of only cPRC1 target genes (PCGF6-CBX7+RING1B+) (blue dot plots in Figure 3C, left; blue lines in Figure 3C, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PCGF6 preferentially recruits RING1B to PCGF6-PRC1 targets, but not to cPRC1 targets.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that PCGF6 preferentially recruits RING1B to PCGF6-PRC1 targets, but not to cPRC1 targets.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing differential effects of Pcgf6 deletion on RING1B binding at different target classes (Figure 3B,C).

claim: PCGF6 H155Y mutant fails to interact with RING1B while retaining the ability to associate with L3MBTL2 and MAX.
source: We expressed the mutant in Pcgf6-KO ESCs, and noted that it indeed failed to interact with RING1B, while retaining the ability to associate with L3MBTL2 and MAX (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PCGF6 H155Y mutant can bind target genes but fails to recruit RING1B.
source: ChIP-qPCR analysis showed that although the mutant PCGF6 could bind the indicated target genes, it failed to recruit RING1B (Figure 3D) and, as a result, H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 marks were also not established in the target genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PCGF6 H155Y mutant fails to repress PCGF6-PRC1 target genes.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the mutant PCGF6 failed to repress PCGF6-PRC1 targets genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PCGF6 contributes to the assembly and recruitment of the PCGF6-PRC1 complex by direct physical interactions with RING1B.
source: Based on these observations, we concluded that PCGF6 contributes to the assembly and recruitment of the PCGF6-PRC1 complex by direct physical interactions with RING1B, which likely plays a critical role to mediate the repression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutant analysis showing that disrupting PCGF6-RING1B interaction abolishes repression (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).

claim: PCGF6 is dispensable for L3MBTL2 binding to gene promoters.
source: Indeed, we noted that PCGF6 was dispensable for L3MBTL2 binding of gene promoters (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 may function in parallel to recruit ncPRC1 complexes.
source: As L3MBTL2 has been reported as a recruiter of ncPRC1 (Qin et al., 2012; Trojer et al., 2011), this observation suggests that PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 may function in parallel to recruit ncPRC1 complexes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that L3MBTL2 binding is independent of PCGF6 (Figure 3E) combined with cited literature on L3MBTL2 function.

claim: H3K9me2 levels at PCGF6-PRC1 targets do not show considerable changes in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
source: We went on to examine contribution of H3K9me2, which is mediated by G9A/GLP, for PCGF6-PRC1-target repression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). Unlike L3mbtl2-KO ESCs (Qin et al., 2012), we did not observe considerable changes in H3K9me2 levels in Pcgf6-KO.
evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The L3MBTL2/G9A axis is marginally involved in PCGF6-mediated repression.
source: Together, we suggest that the L3MBTL2/G9A axis is marginally involved in PCGF6-mediated repression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of H3K9me2 changes in Pcgf6-KO (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: CBX1/3 have a marginal role for the repression of PCGF6-PRC1 targets in ESCs.
source: We did not observe a significant change in the expression levels of PCGF6+CBX7-RING1B+ in Cbx1/3-dKO ESCs, suggesting that CBX1/3 have, if any, a marginal role for the repression of PCGF6-PRC1 targets in ESCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis in Cbx1/3-dKO ESCs shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: H3K27me3 is dispensable for locus-specific recruitment of PCGF6-PRC1.
source: We did not observe any significant differences in FLAG-PCGF6 binding between WT and Eed-KO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that H3K27me3 is dispensable for locus-specific recruitment of PCGF6-PRC1.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data comparing PCGF6 binding in WT and Eed-KO ESCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claim: H2AK119ub1 levels at genes bound by PCGF6 are not affected in Eed-KO ESCs.
source: Consistently, H2AK119ub1 levels at genes bound by PCGF6 were not affected in the Eed-KO (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PCGF2 barely associates with PCGF6 targets irrespective of H3K27me3 status.
source: In contrast, PCGF2, a component of cPRC1, barely associates with PCGF6 targets irrespective of H3K27me3 status, while it strongly associates with cPRC1 targets such as Zic1 and Hoxb3 in an EED-dependent manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The H3K27me3-dependent pathway to recruit cPRC1 is barely active at PCGF6-PRC1 targets.
source: These findings suggests that the H3K27me3-dependent pathway to recruit cPRC1 is barely active at PCGF6-PRC1 targets.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that PCGF2 does not bind PCGF6 targets even when H3K27me3 is present (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The E-box motif CACGTG is enriched within PCGF6-bound promoters.
source: We observed enrichment of the E-box motif CACGTG, a DNA sequence that is recognized by the bHLH-containing transcription factors including MAX (Blackwood and Eisenman, 1991), within these promoters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The E-box motif CACGTG is not enriched in RING1B- or CBX7-bound genes.
source: Importantly, this motif was not enriched in RING1B- or CBX7-bound genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the E-box motif is a feature of PCGF6-PRC1 targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There is considerable overlap between PCGF6-bound and MAX-bound genes.
source: Consistent with this notion, we observed considerable overlap between PCGF6-bound and MAX-bound genes, while the overlap between PCGF6-bound and MYC-bound genes was much less (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: MGA forms a heterodimer with MAX and binds the CACGTG E-box motif.
source: Interestingly, MGA, a transcription factor that also forms a heterodimer with MAX and binds the CACGTG E-box motif (Hurlin et al., 1999), is included in the PCGF6 complex determined by us (Figure 1B) and others (Gao et al., 2012; Hauri et al., 2016; Kloet et al., 2016; Ogawa et al., 2002; Qin et al., 2012; Trojer et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and mass spectrometry data in this study (Figure 1B).

claim: Genes bound by MAX, PCGF6 and RING1B (MAX+PCGF6+RING1B+) show significant up-regulation in Max-KD or Mga-KD ESCs.
source: Interestingly, genes that were bound by MAX, PCGF6 and RING1B (MAX+PCGF6+RING1B+) showed significant up-regulation in Max-KD or Mga-KD ESCs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Genes bound by PCGF6 and RING1B but not MAX (MAX-PCGF6+RING1B+) are barely up-regulated in Max-KD or Mga-KD ESCs.
source: In contrast, genes bound by PCGF6 and RING1B, but not MAX (MAX-PCGF6+RING1B+), were barely up-regulated (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Genes bound only by RING1B (MAX-PCGF6-RING1B+) show significant up-regulation in Max-KD or Mga-KD ESCs.
source: Intriguingly, we observed significant up-regulation of genes bound only by RING1B (MAX-PCGF6-RING1B+).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MAX and MGA primarily contribute to the repression of MAX+PCGF6+RING1B+ genes.
source: We thus suggest MAX and MGA primarily contribute to the repression of MAX+PCGF6+RING1B+ genes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing differential effects of Max/Mga knockdown on different gene categories (Figure 4B).

claim: Genes bound by PCGF6, RING1B and MAX but not by MYC are significantly enriched in germ cell- and meiosis-related functions.
source: GO analysis revealed that genes bound by PCGF6, RING1B and MAX but not by MYC (PCGF6+RING1B+MAX+MYC-), were significantly enriched in germ cell- and meiosis-related functions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), further supporting our model that PCGF6-PRC1 functions as a dedicated repressor of genes associated with germ cells and meiosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: PCGF6 binding to target loci depends on MAX and MGA.
source: Indeed, ChIP-qPCR in the Max-KD or Mga-KD ESCs revealed that PCGF6 binding to target loci depends on MAX and MGA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MAX and MGA bind their targets in mutually dependent manner.
source: Importantly, MAX and MGA bind these targets in mutually dependent manner (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing that knockdown of either Max or Mga reduces binding of both proteins (Figure 4C).

claim: RING1B and RYBP do not bind to PCGF6-PRC1 target loci in Max-KO ESCs.
source: RING1B and RYBP, which form stoichiometric complexes with PCGF6 (Figure 1B), did not bind to PCGF6-PRC1 target loci in the Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Local H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 levels are considerably decreased at PCGF6-PRC1 targets in Max-KO ESCs.
source: Likewise, local H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 levels were considerably decreased, and binding of L3MBTL2, another key regulator of ncPRC1, into PCGF6-PRC1 target genes was also depleted in the Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: L3MBTL2 binding to PCGF6-PRC1 target genes is depleted in Max-KO ESCs.
source: Likewise, local H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 levels were considerably decreased, and binding of L3MBTL2, another key regulator of ncPRC1, into PCGF6-PRC1 target genes was also depleted in the Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Enrichment of RING1B, H2AK119ub1, H3K27me3 and RYBP at Zic1 (a cPRC1 target) does not show considerable changes in Max-KO ESCs.
source: In contrast, enrichment of RING1B, H2AK119ub1, H3K27me3 and RYBP at Zic1, a cPRC1 target, did not show considerable changes in the Max-KO ESCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Recruitment of both PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 requires MAX.
source: These results suggest that recruitment of both PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 requires MAX.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ChIP-qPCR data showing loss of both PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 binding in Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4D).

claim: The MAX/MGA heterodimer recruits PCGF6-PRC1 to its targets.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that the MAX/MGA heterodimer recruits PCGF6-PRC1 to its targets.
evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including motif enrichment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), MAX/MGA-dependent PCGF6 binding (Figure 4C), and loss of PCGF6-PRC1 components in Max-KO (Figure 4D).

claim: MAX plays a role in maintaining ESC proliferation and self-renewal ability.
source: A role for MAX in maintaining ESC proliferation and self-renewal ability has been reported in a previous study (Hishida et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Conditional deletion of Max leads to slower ESC proliferation and cell differentiation.
source: We also observed that conditional deletion of Max (Max-KO) led to slower ESC proliferation and cell differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Rescuing Max-KO cells with exogenous WT MAX restores cell proliferation and blocks spontaneous differentiation.
source: Rescuing the induced Max-KO cells with an exogenous WT MAX restored cell proliferation and blocked spontaneous differentiation, as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Mutant MAX proteins with defects in the basic region of the bHLH domain fail to rescue Max-KO ESC proliferation defects.
source: In contrast, mutant MAX proteins harboring defects in the basic region of the bHLH (basic helix-loop-helix) domain [hereafter referred to as MAX(VD) or MAX(Δb)] (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, left), failed to do so (Figure 5A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: DNA motif recognition by MAX plays a role in maintaining ESCs by recruiting the PCGF6-PRC1 complex.
source: These findings indicate that DNA motif recognition by MAX plays a role in maintaining ESCs, at least partly by recruiting the PCGF6-PRC1 complex.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MAX mutants defective in DNA binding cannot rescue ESC maintenance (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) combined with evidence that MAX recruits PCGF6-PRC1 (Figure 4C,D).

claim: Mutant MAX proteins retain the ability to associate with HA-PCGF6, RING1B and L3MBTL2.
source: Mechanistically, co-IP analyses showed that a FLAG-tagged MAX protein physically interacts with HA-PCGF6, RING1B and L3MBTL2. The mutant MAX proteins also retained the ability to associate and form stable complexes with HA-PCGF6, RING1B and L3MBTL2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: FLAG-tagged MAX can restore binding of HA-tagged PCGF6 to target loci in Max-KO ESCs.
source: As expected, ChIP-qPCR revealed that the FLAG-tagged MAX could restore binding of the HA-tagged PCGF6 into target loci in Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D), whereas the mutant MAX proteins failed to bind targets and recruit HA-tagged PCGF6.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Mutant MAX proteins fail to bind targets and recruit HA-tagged PCGF6.
source: As expected, ChIP-qPCR revealed that the FLAG-tagged MAX could restore binding of the HA-tagged PCGF6 into target loci in Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D), whereas the mutant MAX proteins failed to bind targets and recruit HA-tagged PCGF6.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: The growth rate of Pcgf6-KO ESCs is significantly slower than WT in the presence of 3i and fetal bovine serum.
source: Indeed, the growth rate of Pcgf6-KO ESCs was significantly slower than the WT in the presence of three inhibitors (3i: SU5402 for FGFR, PD184352 for ERK, and CHIR99021 for GSK3) and fetal bovine serum as suggested previously (Zdzieblo et al., 2014) (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The growth of Pcgf6-KO ESCs is further halted under serum-free condition.
source: The growth of Pcgf6-KO ESCs was further halted under serum-free condition (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Pcgf6-KO ESCs maintain an ESC-like morphology.
source: Unlike the Max-KO, however, Pcgf6-KO ESCs maintained an ESC-like morphology.
evidence: This claim is supported by phase-contrast microscopy images shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PCGF6-PRC1 has a role in ESC proliferation but may not be essential to maintain ES cell morphology.
source: These findings support the notion that PCGF6-PRC1 has a role in ESC proliferation, but may not be essential to maintain ES cell morphology.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Pcgf6-KO ESCs grow slowly but maintain ESC morphology (Figure 5A,B,D).

claim: Genetic ablation of Pcgf6 at ESC stage induces growth arrest and cell death.
source: Genetic ablation of Pcgf6 at day −5 induced growth arrest and cell death of ESCs (Figure 5D); while ablation of Pcgf6 at day −2 caused significant growth defects in epiLCs (Figure 5E), revealing a stage-specific role of PCGF6 for growth and survival of ESCs and epiLCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Ablation of Pcgf6 at epiLC stage causes significant growth defects.
source: Genetic ablation of Pcgf6 at day −5 induced growth arrest and cell death of ESCs (Figure 5D); while ablation of Pcgf6 at day −2 caused significant growth defects in epiLCs (Figure 5E), revealing a stage-specific role of PCGF6 for growth and survival of ESCs and epiLCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: OHT-treatment at post-epiLC stage does not induce growth arrest or cell death and even accelerates differentiation and proliferation.
source: In contrast, OHT-treatment at day +2 (post-epiLC stage) did not induce growth arrest or cell death and, surprisingly, even accelerated differentiation and proliferation (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis and cell proliferation data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The same group of genes (PCGF6+RING1B+ category) are de-repressed in ESCs, epiLCs and PGCLCs in the absence of Pcgf6.
source: We observed that the same group of genes (the PCGF6+RING1B+ category in ESCs) were de-repressed in ESCs, epiLCs and PGCLCs in the absence of Pcgf6.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The extent of derepression of PCGF6 target genes is similar among ESCs, epiLCs and PGCLCs.
source: Furthermore, the extent of derepression of PCGF6 target genes was also similar among these three cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: PCGF6-PRC1-mediated gene silencing is essential to maintain ESC and epiLC, but not PGCLC.
source: Thus, these results indicate that the different phenotypic impacts of Pcgf6 ablation in ESCs, epiLCs and PGCLCs are not due to up-regulation of different sets of genes, but rather suggest that PCGF6-PRC1-mediated gene silencing is essential to maintain ESC and epiLC, but not PGCLC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that similar genes are de-repressed in all three cell types (Figure 5G) but only ESCs and epiLCs show growth defects (Figure 5D,E,F).

claim: PCGF6 plays a role in maintaining pluripotency by suppressing germ cell potential in ESCs.
source: PCGF6, therefore, plays a role in maintaining pluripotency, likely by suppressing germ cell potential in ESCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that PCGF6 represses germ cell genes and is required for ESC maintenance but not PGCLC maintenance (Figure 5).

claim: Pcgf6 is expressed in broad range of tissues and cell types and abundantly in testis, ESCs and pre-implantation embryos.
source: Consistently, Pcgf6 is expressed in broad range of tissues and cell types and even abundantly in testis, ESCs and pre-implantation embryos (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Pcgf6-KO mice are viable and fertile.
source: We found that Pcgf6-KO (−/−) mice were viable and fertile, but were not born at the normal Mendelian ratio (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by genotype distribution data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Pcgf6-KO mice are not born at the normal Mendelian ratio.
source: We found that Pcgf6-KO (−/−) mice were viable and fertile, but were not born at the normal Mendelian ratio (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by genotype distribution data showing deviation from expected 1:2:1 ratio (Figure 6D).

claim: Lethality among Pcgf6−/− homozygous embryos can be observed as early as the blastocyst stage (3.5 dpc).
source: Lethality among Pcgf6−/− homozygous embryos could be observed as early as the blastocyst stage [3.5 days post coitum (dpc)].
evidence: This claim is supported by genotype distribution data at different developmental stages (Figure 6D).

claim: Embryonic death in the Pcgf6−/− line can be continuously detected during post-implantation development.
source: Furthermore, embryonic death in the Pcgf6−/− line could be continuously detected during post-implantation development.
evidence: This claim is supported by genotype distribution data at different developmental stages (Figure 6D).

claim: About one third of the surviving Pcgf6−/− embryos at 10.5 dpc exhibit growth retardation.
source: Consistently, we found that about one third of the surviving Pcgf6−/− embryos at 10.5 dpc exhibited growth retardation (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by embryo images shown in Figure 6E.

claim: No ESC lines could be established from Pcgf6−/− blastocysts.
source: From 73 blastocysts collected, we could establish 22 ESC-like lines. Remarkably, among these 22 lines, not a single one was homozygous Pcgf6−/− (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the ESC derivation data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Pcgf6-deficient ICMs are functionally different from WT ICMs.
source: As ESCs could not be established from Pcgf6−/− lines, we surmised that Pcgf6-deficient ICMs are functionally different from their WT counterparts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the failure to establish ESC lines from Pcgf6−/− blastocysts (Figure 6F).

claim: PCGF6 has a role in both pre- and peri-implantation development.
source: Collectively, these results reveal a role for PCGF6 in both pre- and peri-implantation development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the embryonic lethality data (Figure 6D,E) and failure to establish ESC lines (Figure 6F).

claim: Pcgf6−/− mice exhibit morphological alterations of the vertebrae that represent anterior transformations of the axis.
source: Intriguingly, we observed morphological alterations of the vertebrae that represent anterior transformations of the axis in these mice (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by skeletal analysis shown in Figure 6G,H.

claim: PCGF6 over-expression induces posterior transformations of the axis.
source: To further confirm the role of PCGF6 for A-P patterning, we then tested the impacts of PCGF6 over-expression and, indeed, observed posterior transformations of the axis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by skeletal analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Skeletal alterations in Pcgf6−/− mice are accompanied by aberrant repression of Hoxb6 at the eighth pre-vertebra.
source: We further found that skeletal alterations in Pcgf6−/− mice were accompanied by aberrant repression of Hoxb6 at the eighth pre-vertebra (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: PCGF6 regulates A-P patterning presumably through regulation of Hox genes.
source: These suggest that PCGF6 regulates A-P patterning presumably through regulation of Hox genes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of skeletal transformations (Figure 6G,H) and altered Hoxb6 expression (Figure 6I).

claim: Anterior transformations in Pcgf6−/− mice are suppressed by the Pcgf2 mutation.
source: We indeed observed that anterior transformations in Pcgf6−/− mice were suppressed by the Pcgf2 mutation, suggesting mutually counteracting properties of PCGF6 and PCGF2.
evidence: This claim is supported by skeletal analysis of double mutants shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Pcgf6−/− mice show significant reduction of placental size.
source: In addition to the skeletal phenotypes, we also noted significant reduction of placental size, manifested by hypoplasticity and malformation of the labyrinth layer, in the Pcgf6−/− mice (Figure 6J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 6J,K.

claim: The number of spongiotrophoblast cells and trophoblast giant cells is dramatically decreased in Pcgf6−/− mice.
source: In particular, the number of spongiotrophoblast cells and trophoblast giant cells (TGCs), identified by expression of Pl1 (placental lactogen-I, also known as Prl3d1) and Tpbpa (trophoblast specific protein alpha), respectively, was dramatically decreased.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: PCGF6 has roles in peri-implantation development, including A-P specification and regulation of placental development.
source: These findings demonstrate further roles of PCGF6 in peri-implantation development, including A-P specification and regulation of placental development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the skeletal phenotypes (Figure 6G,H,I) and placental defects (Figure 6J,K) observed in Pcgf6−/− mice.

claim: PCGF6 constitutes a non-canonical PRC1 complex that includes the core PRC1 component RING1B.
source: In the present study, we show that PCGF6 constitutes a non-canonical PRC1 complex, PCGF6-PRC1, that includes the core PRC1 component RING1B.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry (Figure 1A,B) and co-IP data (Figure 1C).

claim: PCGF6 physically interacts with RING1B and plays a role in recruitment of RING1B to target genes.
source: PCGF6 physically interacts with RING1B, and plays a role in recruitment of RING1B to target genes, followed by deposition of H2AK119ub1 and transcriptional silencing.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data (Figure 1C), ChIP-seq showing RING1B loss in Pcgf6-KO (Figure 3B,C), and mutant analysis (Figure 3D).

claim: PCGF6-PRC1 recruits PRC2 to target genes.
source: We have previously reported that the PCGF1-associated ncPRC1 (PCGF1-PRC1) recruits PRC2 to target genes (Blackledge et al., 2014). Here, we demonstrate that PCGF6-PRC1 also has a similar role, as ectopic targeting of a PCGF6 protein fused to the Tet repressor (PCGF6/TETR) to a pre-integrated TetO array leads to sequential binding of RING1B, H2AK119ub1 deposition and PRC2 recruitment in cis (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the tethering experiment shown in Figure 3A and cited previous work.

claim: PCGF6-PRC1-mediated targeting of PRC2 takes place at endogenous genomic loci, particularly at promoters of genes enriched for germ cell-specific and meiosis-specific functions.
source: Like PCGF1-PRC1, PCGF6-PRC1-mediated targeting of PRC2 also takes place in endogenous genomic loci, in particular at promoters of a certain group of genes that are enriched for germ cell-specific and meiosis-specific functions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 1D-G) and GO analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claim: PCGF6-PRC1 target genes are distinct from those bound by PCGF1-PRC1 and canonical PRC1.
source: However, these genes are distinct from those bound by PCGF1-PRC1 and canonical PRC1, which mainly include developmental genes (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data comparing PCGF6 targets with CBX7 targets (Figure 1D-G).

claim: Developmental genes are evolutionarily conserved targets of PcG complexes and are characterized by long CpG island promoters that are usually not marked by DNA methylation.
source: Such developmental genes are evolutionarily conserved targets of PcG complexes, and are characterized by long CpG island (CGI) promoters that are usually not marked by DNA methylation (Sharif et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: KDM2B recruits PCGF1-PRC1 to developmental genes by binding unmethylated CGIs.
source: The CXXC domain containing protein KDM2B recruits PCGF1-PRC1 into these loci by binding unmethylated CGIs (Blackledge et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PCGF6-PRC1 target loci have slightly shorter and more DNA methylated CGIs compared to developmental genes.
source: In contrast, PCGF6-PRC1 target loci tend to have slightly shorter and more DNA methylated CGIs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), where KDM2B seems to play distinct roles from PCGF1-PRC1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: H3K27me3 depositions at PCGF6-PRC1 targets are less active to recruit cPRC1.
source: Indeed, H3K27me3 depositions at PCGF6-PRC1 targets are less active to recruit cPRC1 though underlying mechanisms await elucidative (Figure 1G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing minimal PCGF2 binding at PCGF6 targets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).

claim: There are at least two major modes of gene silencing by PRC1: one involving PCGF1-PRC1 and cPRC1 silencing developmental genes, and another involving PCGF6-PRC1 silencing germ cell-specific and meiosis-specific genes.
source: Thus, our findings reveal that there are at least two major modes of gene silencing by PRC1; the first involves PCGF1-PRC1 and cPRC1 and silences developmental genes, while the second involves PCGF6-PRC1 and silences germ cell-specific and meiosis-specific genes (see the model in Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comprehensive analysis of PCGF6-PRC1 targets compared to other PRC1 complexes throughout the study.

claim: PCGF6-PRC1 target genes are enriched for the binding motif of the bHLHZ transcription factor MAX.
source: By surveying DNA sequences of the PCGF6-PRC1 target genes, we find that they are enriched for the binding motif of the bHLHZ (basic helix-loop-helix, also containing a leucine zipper) transcription factor MAX (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MAX forms a heterodimer with MGA.
source: Previous reports showed that MAX forms a heterodimer with MGA, another E-box binding protein (Hurlin et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MAX and MGA are directly involved in recruitment of PCGF6-PRC1 to target genes.
source: Interestingly, we identified MGA as a PCGF6 interacting factor by mass-spectrometry (Figure 1A,B), indicating that MAX and MGA may be directly involved in recruitment of PCGF6-PRC1 into target genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 1A,B) and ChIP-qPCR showing MAX/MGA-dependent PCGF6 recruitment (Figure 4C).

claim: Both MAX and MGA are enriched at PCGF6-PRC1 target genes.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, both MAX and MGA were enriched at PCGF6-PRC1 target genes (Figures 1G, 4A and C); and depletion of MAX or MGA by siRNA caused a reduction of PCGF6 binding to these loci (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figures 1G, 4A and C.

claim: The MAX/MGA heterodimer plays a role in recruitment of the ncPRC1 component L3MBTL2.
source: Previous studies show that the MAX/MGA heterodimer also plays a role in recruitment of the ncPRC1 component L3MBTL2 (Suzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MAX/MGA independently associates with PCGF6 or L3MBTL2.
source: Our results demonstrate that MAX/MGA independently associates with PCGF6 or L3MBTL2, as ablation of PCGF6 does not affect binding of L3MBTL2 (Figures 3E and 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figures 3E and 4D.

claim: MAX/MGA represses target genes through multiple mechanisms that may function in parallel.
source: These findings indicate that MAX/MGA represses target genes through multiple mechanisms that may function in parallel.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MAX/MGA recruits both PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 independently (Figures 3E, 4D).

claim: ESCs deficient for MAX or MGA show a more drastic phenotype than Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
source: Consistent with this notion, ESCs deficient for MAX or MGA show a more drastic phenotype than the Pcgf6-KO ESCs (Figure 6A,B,D) (Hishida et al., 2011; Washkowitz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of phenotypes shown in Figure 6A,B,D and citations to previous literature.

claim: L3MBTL2 associates with the H3K9me2 methyltransferases G9A and GLP.
source: Interestingly, L3MBTL2 associates with the H3K9me2 methyltransferases G9A and GLP (Ogawa et al., 2002; Qin et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: G9A and GLP silence germ cell-specific genes in ESCs.
source: As G9A and GLP silence germ cell-specific genes in ESCs (Maeda et al., 2013), we speculate that L3MBTL2 contributes to transcriptional repression of these genes in association with G9A and GLP; while the same group of genes are silenced by a parallel pathway involving PCGF6 and RING1B (see the model in Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: L3MBTL2 contributes to transcriptional repression of germ cell genes in association with G9A and GLP, while the same genes are silenced by a parallel pathway involving PCGF6 and RING1B.
source: As G9A and GLP silence germ cell-specific genes in ESCs (Maeda et al., 2013), we speculate that L3MBTL2 contributes to transcriptional repression of these genes in association with G9A and GLP; while the same group of genes are silenced by a parallel pathway involving PCGF6 and RING1B (see the model in Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the cited literature on G9A/GLP function and the data showing independent recruitment of L3MBTL2 and PCGF6 by MAX/MGA.

claim: The existence of several repressive epigenetic mechanisms targeting germ cell-specific genes suggests the importance of preventing aberrant activation of such genes during pre- and peri-implantation embryonic development.
source: The existence of several repressive epigenetic mechanisms that target germ cell-specific genes suggests the importance of preventing aberrant activation of such genes during pre- and peri-implantation embryonic development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of multiple parallel repressive mechanisms (PCGF6-PRC1 and L3MBTL2/G9A/GLP) targeting the same genes.

claim: Constitutive deletion of Pcgf6 causes impaired development of the placenta, particularly of the spongiotrophoblast layer and trophoblast giant cells.
source: Furthermore, constitutive deletion of Pcgf6 causes impaired development of the placenta, in particular of the spongiotrophoblast layer and trophoblast giant cells (TGCs) (Figure 6J and K).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6J and K.

claim: Aberrant phenotypes are observed in the Pcgf6−/− embryo proper, including defects in anterior-posterior axis specification and ectopic expression of developmental genes such as Hoxb6.
source: Such aberrant phenotypes are also observed in the embryo proper, including defects in anterior-posterior (A-P) axis specification and ectopic expression of developmental genes such as Hoxb6 (Figure 6G, H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by skeletal analysis (Figure 6G,H) and in situ hybridization (Figure 6I).

claim: PCGF6 has a previously unappreciated function for repression of germ cell-specific genes in ESCs.
source: Taken together, we demonstrate a previously unappreciated function of the non-canonical PRC1 component PCGF6 for repression of germ cell-specific genes in ESCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comprehensive analysis of PCGF6 targets and their de-repression in Pcgf6-KO ESCs throughout the study.

claim: Transcriptional silencing of germ cell-specific genes requires the function of RING1B and H2AK119ub1, but not PRC2 and H3K27me3.
source: We further show that transcriptional silencing of such genes requires the function of RING1B and H2AK119ub1, but not PRC2 and H3K27me3.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing RING1B-dependent repression (Figure 2D), H2AK119ub1 requirement (Figure 2C), and limited impact of PRC2 loss (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).

claim: PCGF6-bound genes are enriched for short CGIs, frequently marked by methylated DNA.
source: PCGF6-bound genes are enriched for short CGIs, frequently marked by methylated DNA, and are not bound by PCGF1-PRC1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: PCGF6-bound genes are not bound by PCGF1-PRC1.
source: PCGF6-bound genes are enriched for short CGIs, frequently marked by methylated DNA, and are not bound by PCGF1-PRC1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the distinct characteristics of PCGF6 targets compared to PCGF1-PRC1 targets (developmental genes with long unmethylated CGIs).

claim: Developmental genes, which are the main targets of PCGF1-PRC1, are not bound by PCGF6-PRC1.
source: Indeed, developmental genes, which are the main targets of PCGF1-PRC1, are not bound by PCGF6-PRC1, revealing distinct functional roles of these two ncPRC1 complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing minimal overlap between PCGF6 and CBX7 targets (Figure 1F).

claim: PCGF6-PRC1 is recruited to target sites by the MAX/MGA heterodimer, while PCGF1-PRC1 is recruited by KDM2B.
source: Consistent with this model, PCGF6-PRC1 is recruited to target sites by the MAX/MGA heterodimer, while PCGF1-PRC1 is recruited by the unmethylated CpG binding protein KDM2B (Farcas et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing MAX/MGA-dependent PCGF6 recruitment (Figure 4C) and a citation to previous work on KDM2B-mediated PCGF1-PRC1 recruitment.

claim: This work shows a link between sequence specific DNA binding by the MAX/MGA heterodimer with PRC1-mediated transcriptional silencing of germ cell-specific genes by PCGF6, for regulation of pre- and post-implantation embryonic development.
source: Our work thus shows a link between sequence specific DNA binding by the MAX/MGA heterodimer with PRC1-mediated transcriptional silencing of germ cell-specific genes by PCGF6, for regulation of pre- and post-implantation embryonic development.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study, integrating data on MAX/MGA-dependent PCGF6 recruitment (Figure 4), PCGF6-mediated repression of germ cell genes (Figure 2), and developmental phenotypes (Figure 6).
